lines.text: Today Python becomes a paintbrush. You will steer a turtle with code and turn loops and functions into art.
import turtle opens the drawing toolbox, and t = turtle.Turtle() gives you a turtle with a pen. t.forward(100) moves it 100 steps and draws a line.
The Python Lab shows the drawing next to your output.
t.right(90) turns the turtle 90 degrees clockwise, and t.left(90) turns it the other way.
A full turn is 360 degrees.
For a shape with n sides, turn 360 divided by n at every corner.
A for loop repeats forward and turn to make a shape.
Put that loop inside def draw_polygon(sides, size): and one line can draw any shape. draw_polygon(6, 50) draws a hexagon.
t.color("orange") changes the pen colour. t.penup() lifts the pen so the turtle moves without drawing, and t.pendown() puts it back. t.goto(x, y) jumps to a point on the canvas.
Draw one shape, turn a little, and draw it again.
Do that twelve times and a flower pattern appears.
That is the secret of a rangoli generator.
First we import the turtle toolbox and make a turtle called t.
Forward draws a line, left turns on the spot, and forward again draws the second line.
A square is four sides and four turns of ninety degrees.
Instead of typing eight lines, a loop repeats the two lines four times.
The function takes the number of sides and the size as parameters.
It turns three hundred and sixty divided by the sides, so any shape closes up perfectly.
Color changes the pen, so the next shape is orange.
Pen up lifts the pen, goto jumps to a new spot without drawing, and pen down starts drawing again.
We draw a hexagon, turn thirty degrees, and repeat twelve times to go all the way round.
The remainder sign picks the next colour from the list each time, so the colours take turns.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
